stem: In a client with cirrhosis, portal hypertension promotes formation of portosystemic collateral vessels. Which complication most directly reflects enlargement of those collateral veins?

options.A: Gastroesophageal varices that can rupture and bleed.
options.B: Peripheral edema caused mainly by reduced plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin.
options.C: Prolonged INR caused by reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors.
options.D: Hepatorenal syndrome caused by advanced circulatory and renal dysfunction in decompensated cirrhosis.

rationale: AASLD guidance identifies varices as portosystemic collateral vessels that develop as a direct consequence of portal hypertension. In cirrhosis these collaterals commonly occur in the esophagus and stomach and can rupture, producing variceal hemorrhage. Therefore A most directly reflects enlargement of portosystemic collateral veins. B results primarily from fluid/sodium retention and reduced oncotic pressure, C from impaired hepatic synthetic function, and D from advanced hemodynamic/renal dysfunction rather than collateral-vessel enlargement itself.
educational_objective: Link portal hypertension specifically to formation and enlargement of portosystemic collateral veins, especially gastroesophageal varices with risk of hemorrhage.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
source_document_title: Portal Hypertension Bleeding in Cirrhosis; AASLD Practice Guidance on Risk Stratification and Management of Portal Hypertension and Varices in Cirrhosis
source_version_date: Current AASLD portal-hypertension guidance and 2026 supporting clinical guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: AASLD Portal Hypertension Bleeding in Cirrhosis practice-guidance page: cirrhosis with portal hypertension and varices. AASLD clinical guidance on gastric varices: varices are portosystemic collateral vessels developing as a direct consequence of portal hypertension and commonly occur in esophagus/stomach; variceal hemorrhage is a major portal-hypertension complication.
source_claim_supported: Portal hypertension causes portosystemic collateral vessels/varices; enlargement of gastroesophageal varices creates a direct risk of variceal hemorrhage.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize pathophysiology and complications of chronic liver disease/portal hypertension, identify life-threatening bleeding risks, and intervene for acute deterioration.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — portal hypertension and gastroesophageal varices

source_original.stem: In a client with cirrhosis, portal hypertension promotes formation of portosystemic collateral vessels. Which complication most directly reflects enlargement of those collateral veins?

options.A: Gastroesophageal varices that can bleed as portosystemic collateral veins enlarge.
options.B: Peripheral edema caused mainly by reduced plasma oncotic pressure from low albumin.
options.C: Prolonged INR caused by reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors.
options.D: Hepatorenal syndrome caused by advanced circulatory and renal dysfunction in decompensated cirrhosis.

source_original.rationale: Portal hypertension drives formation and dilation of portosystemic collateral veins, including gastroesophageal varices, which can rupture and bleed. The stem was narrowed to collateral-vessel formation so the keyed complication is anatomically specific and does not create a second-answer problem with other decompensation findings.
source_original.source_detail: Portal hypertension produces portosystemic collaterals including gastroesophageal varices and risk of variceal hemorrhage. Current AASLD portal-hypertension practice guidance rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the portal-collateral construct and key A, tightened the keyed complication to gastroesophageal varices that can rupture/bleed, preserved the anatomical specificity that excludes other cirrhosis complications, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Portal-hypertension collateral vessels and variceal bleeding
audit_findings.source_authority: Current AASLD portal-hypertension guidance; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: AASLD portal-hypertension practice-guidance page and current AASLD explanation of gastric varices as portosystemic collateral vessels
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item deliberately asks which complication most directly reflects collateral-vessel enlargement, excluding other genuine cirrhosis complications caused by different mechanisms.

distractor_audit.B: A cirrhosis complication but not a direct consequence of enlarged collateral veins.
distractor_audit.C: Reflects impaired hepatic synthesis rather than portosystemic collateral enlargement.
distractor_audit.D: Reflects advanced circulatory/renal dysfunction rather than collateral-vein formation.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A is anatomically the enlarged portosystemic collateral-vessel complication described in the stem.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are plausible cirrhosis complications, preserving discrimination by mechanism rather than obvious unrelated distractors.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — chronic liver disease complications and bleeding risk.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked current AASLD portal-hypertension/variceal guidance, all four cirrhosis complications, rationale, objective, ambiguity, cueing and NCSBN mapping. A remained uniquely correct.
